THE BOOK’S A.L. SYRUP

One syrup.
Different trade-offs.

Scanned page 67 · printed page 108
“Jarabe de Azúcar Saturado (A.L.)”

YOUR FRIEND’S SYRUP · SELECTED BY DEFAULT

Weigh the yield. Refine the balance.

Original recipe: 2 cups sugar + ¾ cup water + ¼ teaspoon cream of tartar + 2 teaspoons lemon juice + a pinch of salt. Mix, bring to a simmering boil and cook to 110°C, then cool.

For a repeatable trial, approximate these as 400 g sugar, 180 g water, 1 g cream of tartar, 10 g lemon juice and 0.3 g salt. Cup and spoon weights vary. Use a thermometer, handle hot syrup carefully, and weigh the cooled yield in a tared container. Make small quantities; refrigerate promptly in a clean covered jar and freeze surplus.

540 g is a placeholder yield, not a prediction. Replace it with your actual cooled weight. Scale the other starting ingredients in proportion if changing sugar mass. Temperature alone cannot establish inversion: acidity, time and heating history matter. The model includes the water consumed when sucrose splits into glucose and fructose, plus an estimated 1.8 g minor solids per 400 g sugar. Lemon sugar and other minor solutes are approximated. POD/PAC use sucrose 1/1 and equal glucose–fructose 1.25/1.9. The midpoint is not a measured sugar profile.

This syrup replaces honey in the recipe solver; it is not an exact reconstruction of the book’s A.L. syrup. The original comparison tool remains below.

Choose a formulation

70–71 °Brix in the textbook

Solids are not the same as sweetness. The book assumes dextrose monohydrate at 91% dry matter and glucose powder at 95% (scanned p. 40). Its 1 kg syrup therefore contains approximately 700.16 g dry solids, not 711 g. °Brix is a sucrose-equivalent refractometer reading, not an exact mixed-sugar assay.
Preparation & substitution notes

Weigh the ingredients. Warm the water, gradually dissolve the sugars while stirring, and heat to 85°C following the book’s process (scanned p. 68). Avoid prolonged boiling. Correct evaporation by returning to the intended batch mass with clean hot water. Cool in a clean covered container.

For home use, make small quantities, refrigerate promptly and use soon; freeze surplus in portions. The book’s commercial room-temperature storage protocol is not validated for these home substitutes.

The liquid-glucose option matches dry solids only when its DE and composition resemble the book’s DE 38–40 powder. Corn syrup with added fructose or vanilla is not a neutral one-for-one replacement. Dextrose and suitable glucose syrup have not been verified in the selected Tamimi catalog.

Honey has more monosaccharides than the original blend. Expect a sweeter, softer result and a honey flavour. Match the whole sorbet’s sugar profile after substitution; do not assume a drop-in equivalent.

TURN THE NUMBERS INTO GELATO

The craft
behind the balance.

Formulate → heat → chill → churn.
A useful starting point for your home machine.

DAYS 1 → 3 → 7

Keep the crystals small.

Churn a thoroughly chilled, matured mix in a pre-cooled machine. Transfer promptly into small, shallow pre-chilled tubs (about 250–500 g each). Cover the surface closely and fit a lid; harden immediately in the coldest part of the freezer.

Store at −18°C or colder, preferably colder if your freezer allows it, away from the door. Check with a freezer thermometer. Avoid repeated warming and refreezing: portion the batch before storage and take out only what you will serve. Temper that portion briefly for scooping.

Compare separate tubs on days 1, 3 and 7: note scoop firmness, iciness, graininess and gumminess at the same serving temperature. Tapioca and higher solids may improve body; they cannot eliminate heat-shock damage. Coarse ice and sandy lactose crystals are different faults. These presets are calculated trials, not a guarantee of week-long texture.

01

Weigh & disperse

Use a scale, including for milk and cream. Mix sugar, milk powder and cocoa thoroughly. Slurry the selected tapioca or corn starch in a little cold liquid from the weighed recipe, then combine. After heating, restore evaporated water to the intended final mix mass before chilling; do not add extra milk or sugar.

02

Heat & blend

For dairy recipes, stir continuously and heat the entire mix to 85°C, using a thermometer. Avoid scorching. Blend carefully without splashing. This also hydrates starch. Do not use this home workflow as a validated commercial food-safety plan.

03

Chill & mature

Cool promptly in an ice bath, then refrigerate at 4°C or below. Mature the covered dairy mix for 4–12 hours. Use clean equipment and pasteurized dairy. The mix must be thoroughly cold before churning.

04

Churn & harden

Churn according to your machine’s capacity and instructions; allow room for incorporated air. Transfer to a shallow, pre-chilled covered container and harden in the freezer. Temper briefly before serving: a −18°C home freezer gives a firmer scoop than a gelato cabinet.

For fruit sorbets

Use unsweetened fruit. Heat the weighed water, sugar, selected liquid sweetener and starch mixture to hydrate the starch; cool promptly. Prepare frozen fruit according to its package instructions, including any cooking requirement, then chill and blend into the cold syrup. Churn immediately or refrigerate briefly until ready.

Fruit sugar varies with ripeness. Edit the fruit’s sugar value from a reliable label or measurement. °Brix includes other soluble solids, so using it as sugar concentration is only an approximation. The app’s 28% default is a supermarket trial, below the book’s usual 30–32% fruit formulations.

What the numbers mean

Fat gives richness. Protein supports body and air retention. Solids reduce the water fraction. Lactose contributes solids but can become sandy at excessive levels.

POD is an estimated sweetness index, and PAC is an estimated sugar-only freezing-point-depression index. Values are grams of sucrose equivalent per 100 g of mix; they are not a predicted freezing or serving temperature. Minerals, sugar mixtures and processing add uncertainty.

TRACEABLE, WITH LIMITS

Sources & assumptions

October trial update

Linked Tamimi listings and pack photos checked 3 October 2026. Rainbow’s pack image provides 28% fat, 24% protein and 39% lactose; 97% solids is estimated. The sugar link is Tamimi Markets, not Alosra; the nut link is hazelnuts, not pistachios. Tapioca’s listing has no usable pack image, so a clearly labelled placeholder is shown. Availability in Jeddah is not confirmed.

Hintz gives cocoa fat at 10–12%. Lindt UK gives 46 g fat, 9.2 g protein and 17 g sugars per 100 g; Saudi packaging may differ. Nielsen-Massey provides the vanilla image and ingredients; its volume-based sugar declaration does not establish sugar per 100 g. Vanilla, hazelnut, coffee and tapioca composition remain editable estimates.

Seven-day texture rationale

University of Guelph: shelf life, hardening, and ageing. Stable cold storage and rapid hardening limit recrystallization; stabilizers retard rather than prevent crystal growth. The app’s 9–10.5% fat, 4.3% protein, 22% sugars, 37–42% solids check, 0.6% tapioca and 80 g/kg syrup are practical starting choices, not published optimal values or validated shelf-life claims.

Your scanned Italian gelato textbook

Scanned pp. 36–50: balance framework; pp. 38–42: 6.6–7% fat, approximately 3.9–4.5% protein and 24.5–25.4% book “total sugars.” P. 40: representative dry matter. Pp. 51–55: fruit formulations. Pp. 58–62: dairy bases. Pp. 67–68: A.L. syrup. Pp. 71–81: flavour examples. Scan page numbers differ from printed page numbers.

Calculation assumptions

Milk, cream and Nido fat, protein and total sugar values were verified from Tamimi package images. Milk per-volume values are converted with an estimated density. Nutella macros are read from Danube’s label image. Régilait macros are derived from its prepared-serving label using 25 g powder per 250 ml. Président’s 35.1% fat is a pack minimum; its other macros are estimated. Danube Almarai cream uses the matching Tamimi pack values, subject to verification. Other grocery composition and all moisture/total-solids values are estimates, editable in Your ingredients. No preset has been kitchen-tested. Starch is not equivalent to commercial “neutro,” and honey is not equivalent to dextrose/glucose powder. For POD/PAC, sucrose = 1/1; lactose = 0.16/1; honey sugars ≈ 1.25/1.9; fruit sugars ≈ 1.15/1.5. Syrup glucose dry solids use an approximate 0.5/0.8 and dextrose dry solids 0.7/1.9. These coefficients are formulation estimates, not values printed on retail nutrition labels.
